common_name: Summer Sun False Sunflower (Semi-Double Golden Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Summer Sun blooms heavily from midsummer into fall on sturdy, self-supporting stems.

directions: Grow in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Summer Sun is a German-bred selection prized for its semi-double, golden-yellow daisy flowers with slightly deeper gold centers, produced in heavier profusion than the wild species over a long midsummer-to-fall bloom window. It holds up well to heat and humidity once established and rarely needs staking despite its substantial height. Deadhead spent blooms to prolong flowering and prevent excessive self-seeding, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring. Its abundant, pollen-rich flowers draw bees and butterflies steadily through the season, and it combines well with ornamental grasses and other late-summer prairie perennials.

common_name: Loraine Sunshine False Sunflower (White-Marbled Variegated Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; foliage variegation is most striking with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Site in average, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, giving some afternoon relief in hot climates to keep the foliage from scorching. Loraine Sunshine is grown chiefly for its dramatic silver-white leaves etched with contrasting dark-green veins, a variegation pattern that persists all season on compact, well-behaved clumps, while single golden-yellow daisy flowers with dark centers appear from midsummer into fall as a secondary feature. It is shorter and slower to spread than the straight species, making it useful as a front-of-border accent plant valued as much for foliage contrast as for bloom. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous, and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly to preserve the variegation.

common_name: Bressingham Doubloon False Sunflower (Double Golden-Orange Heliopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the heavy fully double flowers benefit from a sheltered site or light staking in windy gardens.

directions: Plant in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bressingham Doubloon is a classic English-bred selection producing fully double, deep golden-orange, pompon-like flowers rather than the single daisy form of the wild species, giving an especially rich, dense look in the summer border. Its sturdy stems generally stand upright on their own, though a light support ring helps in exposed or windy sites where the heavy flowerheads can lean. Regular deadheading keeps the long bloom season, from midsummer into early fall, running strongly and tidy. Divide clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering, and expect somewhat less pollinator visitation than single-flowered forms since the extra petals reduce accessible pollen.
sources: American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; pinch stems in late spring to encourage bushier, less floppy growth on this taller heirloom selection.

directions: Grow in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, as sneezeweed performs poorly if allowed to dry out. Riverton Beauty is an early-twentieth-century American heirloom selection bearing warm golden-yellow, reflexed-petal daisy flowers surrounding a distinctive dark mahogany-brown central cone, blooming from late summer into fall. Its height makes it a good candidate for the middle to back of a moist border or rain garden; pinching young stems back by several inches in late spring encourages bushier, sturdier growth and reduces the need for staking. Like other Helenium selections, it draws abundant native bees during its pollen-rich bloom period and benefits from division every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring in moist to wet, fertile soil in partial shade; foliage color is brightest in spring and can scorch or fade to green if exposed to hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in early spring in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade, since this golden-leaved selection scorches readily if grown in hot, dry, or overly sunny spots. Aurea emerges in spring with striking bright chartreuse-to-gold pinnate foliage that provides months of foliage color before the leaves gradually mellow toward green as summer heat increases, with creamy-white, honey-scented flower plumes appearing in mid to late summer much like the species. It is smaller and slightly less vigorous than plain green-leaved meadowsweet, making it a good fit for the moist shade or woodland-edge border, streamside planting, or rain garden where its bright foliage can brighten a shaded corner. Water generously during dry spells, divide congested clumps every few years in spring, and remove any reverted all-green shoots to keep the golden color true.
